questions.question: In a computer system, a running program stores currently required data in RAM. What does RAM stand for?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Random Access Memory**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **RAM** stands for **Random Access Memory**, which serves as the **primary memory** or **main memory** of a computer system.
 
• It is called **Random Access** because any **memory cell** or storage location can be accessed directly by the **CPU** in the same amount of time, regardless of its physical position, unlike **sequential access** devices like **magnetic tapes**.
 
• The **RAM** stores the **operating system**, **application programs**, and data currently in use so that they can be quickly reached by the **processor**.
 
• It is **volatile memory**, meaning that all the information stored in **RAM** is lost as soon as the **power supply** is switched off or the system is **rebooted**.
 
• **RAM** is a **Read/Write memory**, which allows the computer to both read existing data and write new data into it at extremely high speeds.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of RAM:**

 
 
• **SRAM (Static Random Access Memory):** It uses **transistors** to store data and does not need to be **refreshed** periodically. It is faster and more expensive than **DRAM** and is primarily used as **Cache Memory**.
 
• **DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory):** It stores data using **capacitors** and **transistors**. Since capacitors leak charge, **DRAM** must be **refreshed** thousands of times per second. It is used as the main **system memory**.
 
• **SDRAM (Synchronous DRAM):** This type **synchronizes** its speed with the **system clock**, allowing the **CPU** to process instructions more efficiently.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with ROM:**
 
 
• Unlike **RAM**, **ROM (Read Only Memory)** is **non-volatile**, meaning it retains its data even after power is lost. It typically contains the **BIOS (Basic Input/Output System)** necessary for the computer to start up.
 
 
 
• **Capacity and Speed:**
 
 
• Modern **RAM** capacity is measured in **Gigabytes (GB)**, and its speed is often measured in **Megahertz (MHz)** or **Megatransfers per second (MT/s)**. Higher capacity and speed allow for better **multitasking** performance.

questions.question: "Appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in regard to civil matters" is provided in which of the following provisions of the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 133**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 133** of the **Constitution of India** defines the **appellate jurisdiction** of the **Supreme Court** in appeals from **High Courts** specifically regarding **civil matters**.
 
• According to this provision, an appeal lies to the **Supreme Court** from any **judgment, decree, or final order** in a civil proceeding of a **High Court** if the High Court certifies under **Article 134A** that the case involves a **substantial question of law of general importance**.
 
• The High Court must also be of the opinion that the said question needs to be decided by the **Supreme Court** to grant the certificate.
 
• Prior to the **30th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1972**, civil appeals were allowed if the amount or value of the subject matter of the dispute was not less than **20,000 rupees**; however, this monetary requirement was abolished, and the focus shifted entirely to the **substantial question of law**.
 
• Under clause (2) of **Article 133**, any party appealing to the **Supreme Court** may also argue that a substantial question of law as to the **interpretation of the Constitution** has been wrongly decided.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 131**:

 
 
• Specifies the **Original Jurisdiction** of the **Supreme Court**.
 
• It empowers the court to hear disputes between the **Government of India** and one or more **States**, or between two or more **States**, to the exclusion of any other court.
 
 
 
• **Article 132**:
 
 
• Deals with the **appellate jurisdiction** of the **Supreme Court** in appeals from **High Courts** in certain cases involving **constitutional matters**.
 
• It applies if the High Court certifies that the case involves a **substantial question of law** regarding the **interpretation of the Constitution**.
 
 
 
• **Article 134**:
 
 
• Delineates the **appellate jurisdiction** of the **Supreme Court** in **criminal matters**.
 
• It provides for an appeal if a **High Court** has, on appeal, reversed an order of acquittal and sentenced an accused to **death**, or has withdrawn a trial to itself and awarded a death sentence.

questions.question: The ‘Mesolithic Age’ is regarded as a transitional phase because it represents the shift between which two prehistoric periods?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Palaeolithic Age and Neolithic Age**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Mesolithic Age**, often referred to as the **Middle Stone Age**, represents a crucial cultural and technological bridge between the **Palaeolithic Age** (Old Stone Age) and the **Neolithic Age** (New Stone Age).
 
• This period is termed **transitional** because it reflects the shift from the hunter-gatherer lifestyle of the **Pleistocene** epoch to the food-producing, sedentary societies of the **Holocene** epoch.
 
• Geographically and climatically, it coincided with the end of the last **Ice Age** around **10,000 BCE**, leading to warmer climates, increased rainfall, and the expansion of forests and grasslands.
 
• Technologically, it is defined by the production of **microliths**, which are very small, geometric stone tools made of **chert**, **chalcedony**, or **agate**, typically measuring 1 to 5 cm in length.
 
• The economy of the **Mesolithic** people remained based on **hunting, fishing, and gathering**, but it also saw the earliest evidence of **animal domestication**, particularly the **dog**, which paved the way for the agricultural revolution.
 
• Prominent **Mesolithic** sites in India include **Bagor** in Rajasthan, **Adamgarh** in Madhya Pradesh, and **Langhnaj** in Gujarat, providing evidence of both microlithic industries and early burials.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Palaeolithic Age**:

 
 
• The earliest period of human history, characterized by the use of crude, unpolished stone tools like **hand-axes** and **cleavers**.
 
• Humans were entirely **nomadic** and relied on hunting large animals and gathering wild plants during the **Ice Age**.
 
 
 
• **Neolithic Age**:
 
 
• Marked by the **Neolithic Revolution**, where humans began **settled agriculture** and **pottery** making.
 
• Tools became **polished** and **grounded** for higher efficiency in farming and construction.
 
 
 
• **Chalcolithic Age**:
 
 
• Known as the **Copper-Stone Age**, it marked the first use of **metals** alongside stone tools.
 
• It serves as the transition between the **Neolithic** and the **Bronze Age**.
 
 
 
• **Iron Age**:
 
 
• Characterized by the widespread smelting of **iron ore**, leading to the creation of stronger tools and weapons.
 
• In the Indian context, it is often associated with the **Painted Grey Ware (PGW)** culture and the **Vedic period**.

• **Distinct Features of Mumbai Art Deco:**

• **Tropical Motifs:** Buildings often incorporate **bas-reliefs** depicting **palm trees**, sunbursts, and local agricultural scenes, grounding the global style in the **Indian context**.

questions.question: Which day is celebrated as National Youth Day (Birthday of Swami Vivekananda) in India every year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**January 12th**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **National Youth Day**, also known as **Rashtriya Yuva Diwas**, is observed every year on **January 12** to celebrate the birth anniversary of **Swami Vivekananda**, one of India's most influential spiritual leaders.
 
• The **Government of India** officially declared this day in **1984**, and the first nationwide celebration took place on **January 12, 1985**, to inspire the youth of the country.
 
• The primary objective of the day is to propagate the philosophy and ideals of **Swami Vivekananda** among the **Indian youth**, encouraging them to contribute to the nation's progress with energy and character.
 
• **Swami Vivekananda** was born on **January 12, 1863**, in **Kolkata**; his teachings focus on **self-reliance**, **spirituality**, and the potential of the youth to transform society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Swami Vivekananda and his Legacy**:

 
 
• He was the chief disciple of the mystic **Ramakrishna Paramahansa** and established the **Ramakrishna Mission** in **1897** to provide social service and spiritual education.
 
• He gained global recognition after his historic speech at the **Parliament of the World's Religions** in **Chicago** in **1893**, where he introduced **Vedanta** and **Yoga** to the West.
 
• His works and speeches, such as 'Karma Yoga' and 'Raja Yoga', remain fundamental texts for modern spiritual and philosophical study.
 
 
 
• **Other Notable Observances**:
 
 
• **March 20th**: This day is celebrated globally as **World Sparrow Day** to raise awareness about the conservation of sparrows and as the **International Day of Happiness**.
 
• **April 30th**: Observed as **Ayushman Bharat Diwas** in India, highlighting the goals of the **Ayushman Bharat** scheme to provide health insurance to the underprivileged.

questions.question: Which statement accurately explains the nature of the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)?

options.text: It forms a cold frontal region near the Himalayan ranges.
It is an equatorial low-pressure belt where trade winds meet.
It represents a zone of high pressure located near the poles.
It marks a westerly wind system close to the Tropic of Capricorn.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is an equatorial low-pressure belt where trade winds meet.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)** is a permanent **low-pressure belt** encircling the Earth near the **Equator**, where the solar insolation is maximum throughout the year.
 
• It is the region where the **Northeast trade winds** from the Northern Hemisphere and the **Southeast trade winds** from the Southern Hemisphere converge, forcing the air to rise into the atmosphere.
 
• As the converged air mass rises due to **convection**, it cools adiabatically, leading to the formation of towering **cumulonimbus clouds** and frequent, intense **thunderstorms**.
 
• The ITCZ is not stationary; it migrates North or South depending on the **apparent movement of the Sun**. For instance, during the Northern summer, it moves over the **Indian subcontinent**, establishing the **Monsoon Trough**.
 
• Due to the vertical movement of air rather than horizontal flow, this zone is often characterized by very light or calm winds, traditionally known to sailors as the **Doldrums**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Climatic Significance**

 
 
• **Hadley Cell**: The ITCZ represents the ascending branch of the **Hadley Cell**, a major component of the Earth’s **atmospheric circulation** system.
 
• **Monsoon Connection**: The shift of the ITCZ to about **20°N−25°N** latitude over India in July is a primary driver for the **Southwest Monsoon**.
 
• **Precipitation**: This belt is responsible for the high annual rainfall found in **tropical rainforest** regions like the **Amazon Basin** and the **Congo Basin**.
 
 
 
• **Distinction from other zones**
 
 
• **High-Pressure Belts**: Unlike the ITCZ, the **Subtropical Highs** (Horse Latitudes) and **Polar Highs** are regions of descending air and high atmospheric pressure.
 
• **Westerlies**: These are prevailing winds in the **mid-latitudes** (between 30° and 60°), which flow towards the poles, unlike the trade winds that converge at the ITCZ.
 
• **Frontal Systems**: **Cold fronts** and warm fronts are features of the **Extra-tropical Cyclones** in temperate regions, whereas the ITCZ is a thermal, tropical phenomenon.

questions.question: Heat generated in an electrical resistor is measured in which SI unit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Joule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Heat generated in an electrical resistor is a form of **thermal energy** produced by the collision of electrons with the atoms of the resistive material.
 
• The **International System of Units (SI)** identifies the **Joule (J)** as the standard unit for all forms of **energy**, **work**, and **heat**.
 
• The relationship between electricity and heat is defined by **Joule's Law of Heating**, which states that the heat produced (**H**) in a conductor is equal to the product of the square of the **current (I)**, the **resistance (R)**, and the **time (t)** for which the current flows.
 
• The mathematical expression for this law is **H = I²Rt**, where the resulting energy is measured in **Joules**.
 
• One **Joule** is defined as the work done or energy transferred when a force of one **Newton** moves an object through a distance of one **meter** in the direction of the force.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Coulomb**:

 
 
• It is the SI unit of **electric charge**.
 
• One **Coulomb** represents the amount of charge transported by a constant current of one **Ampere** in one **second**.
 
 
 
• **Watt**:
 
 
• It is the SI unit of **power**, which defines the rate at which energy is consumed or converted.
 
• One **Watt** is equivalent to one **Joule per second** (1 W = 1 J/s). While heat is energy (Joules), the rate at which a resistor generates heat is measured in Watts.
 
 
 
• **Volt**:
 
 
• It is the SI unit of **electric potential**, **potential difference**, and **electromotive force (EMF)**.
 
• One **Volt** is defined as the potential difference across a conductor when a current of one **Ampere** dissipates one **Watt** of power.

questions.question: When was the Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) adopted in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1956**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) of 1956** was adopted by the Indian Parliament in **April 1956**, replacing the previous 1948 resolution to align with the goal of a **socialist pattern of society**.
 
• This resolution is famously regarded as the **Economic Constitution of India** because it provided the basic framework for the country's industrial strategy for several decades.
 
• The policy categorized industries into three distinct schedules: **Schedule A** (17 industries under exclusive state responsibility), **Schedule B** (12 industries progressively state-owned but supplemented by the private sector), and **Schedule C** (remaining industries left to the private sector).
 
• It aimed to accelerate the rate of **economic growth** and speed up **industrialization**, specifically focusing on the development of **heavy industries** and machine-making sectors.
 
• The **IPR 1956** emphasized the **Public Sector** taking the lead role, ensuring that the government controlled the **commanding heights of the economy** to prevent the concentration of wealth.
 
• It provided the theoretical and legal basis for the **Second Five-Year Plan**, which was built upon the **Mahalanobis Model** of development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Second Five-Year Plan (1956–1961)**:

 
 
• Formulated by **Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis**, it prioritized **heavy industrialization** over agriculture.
 
• Focus was placed on **iron and steel** plants, **chemical industries**, and **mining** to build a self-reliant economy.
 
 
 
• **Regional Balanced Development**:
 
 
• The **IPR 1956** used **industrial licensing** as a tool to promote regional equality by offering **tax concessions** and lower **electricity tariffs** to industries set up in **backward regions**.
 
 
 
• **Small Scale Industries (SSI)**:
 
 
• In **1955**, the **Karve Committee** (Village and Small-scale Industries Committee) highlighted the potential of **small-scale industries** for rural development.
 
• The 1956 resolution protected these industries by **reserving products** and providing **subsidies** to generate mass employment.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Development and Regulation Act (IDRA), 1951**:
 
 
• This legislative act provided the government with the necessary powers to **regulate** and **license** new and existing industrial units according to the priorities of the 1956 resolution.

questions.question: As of 1 March 2001, what was the population of India?

• As of this reference date, the total population of **India** was recorded at **1,027,015,247**, which is approximately **1,027 million** or **1.027 billion**.
 
• This census officially confirmed that **India** had crossed the **one billion** mark, making it the second country in the world after **China** to reach this demographic threshold.
 
• The population comprised **532.1 million males** and **494.8 million females**, reflecting the vast human resource and demographic diversity of the nation at the start of the **21st century**.

• The **decadal growth rate** from **1991 to 2001** was **21.54%**, showing a slight decline compared to the previous decade.
 
• The **population density** in **2001** was **324 persons per square kilometer**, increasing significantly from **267** in **1991**.
 
• The **sex ratio** was recorded as **933 females per 1,000 males**, showing a marginal improvement from **927** in the **1991 Census**.
 
 
 
• **Literacy and States**:
 
 
• The **literacy rate** in **2001** stood at **64.84%**, with **Kerala** maintaining the highest literacy and **Uttar Pradesh** being the most populous state.
 
• The subsequent **2011 Census** recorded the population at **1,210 million**, continuing the trend of substantial demographic expansion.

questions.question: The Morley-Minto Reforms were introduced by the British Government in India in ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1909**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Morley-Minto Reforms**, officially known as the **Indian Councils Act 1909**, were enacted by the British Parliament to introduce limited self-governance and increase Indian participation in the legislative process.
 
• The reforms were named after **Lord John Morley**, the then **Secretary of State for India**, and **Lord Minto**, who served as the **Viceroy of India** from **1905 to 1910**.
 
• A defining and historically significant feature of the Act was the introduction of **separate electorates** for Muslims, a system where Muslim representatives were elected exclusively by Muslim voters.
 
• The Act significantly increased the size of the legislative councils at both the Central and Provincial levels; for instance, the membership of the **Central Legislative Council** was expanded from **16 to 60**.
 
• It empowered members of the council to ask **supplementary questions** and move resolutions on the budget, although they could not vote on the entire budget.

• **Background and Evolution of Reforms:**

• Due to the institutionalization of communal representation, **Lord Minto** is formally recognized in Indian history as the **Father of Communal Electorate**.
 
• The political trajectory established in **1909** was followed by the **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms** in **1919**, which introduced **Dyarchy** and a **bicameral legislature** at the center.
 
• Later, the **Government of India Act 1935** further expanded the constitutional framework by proposing an **All-India Federation** and granting **Provincial Autonomy**, marking a major step toward the eventual independence of India.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Input and Output devices and select the correct option.

(i) A microphone is an input device that can capture sound, but it cannot output any sound.

(ii) The CPU's processing speed is much faster than the data transfer rate of external devices like printers.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**(i) True, (ii) True**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Microphone** is a specialized **transducer** designed to convert sound waves (acoustic energy) into **electrical signals** (analog or digital) for computer processing; since its hardware architecture is strictly unidirectional for data entry and lacks the components to convert electrical signals back into audible sound waves, it is classified solely as an **input device**. Hence, statement (i) is correct.
 
• The **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** operates at extremely high speeds, with clock rates typically measured in **Gigahertz (GHz)**, which allows it to process billions of operations per second, while external peripherals like **printers** are limited by **mechanical constraints** and the relatively slower data transfer rates of **I/O interfaces** (like USB or Wi-Fi). Hence, statement (ii) is correct.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Input Devices**:

 
 
• These hardware components allow users to feed data into a computer system.
 
• Key examples include **Keyboards** (text entry), **Optical Scanners** (image digitization), and **Joysticks** (control signals).
 
• The primary function is to translate human-understandable data into **binary format**.
 
 
 
• **Output Devices**:
 
 
• These devices receive data from the computer and convert it into a form that is perceptible to humans.
 
• Common examples include **Monitors** (visual), **Printers** (hard copy), and **Speakers** (audio).
 
• While a microphone captures sound, a **Speaker** or **Headset** is required to output it.
 
 
 
• **Speed Gap Management**:
 
 
• Because the **CPU** is significantly faster than I/O devices, computers use **Buffering** and **Spooling** techniques.
 
• A **Buffer** is a temporary storage area in **RAM** that holds data while it is being transferred between two devices with different speeds.
 
• **Print Spooling** allows the CPU to offload a print job to the **Hard Drive** or **Memory** so the user can continue working while the slow printer catches up.

questions.question: A gastrointestinal disease caused by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica leads to abdominal pain and stools with excess mucous and blood clots. It often spreads through contaminated food and water via houseflies acting as mechanical carriers. Which disease is described?

• The parasite primarily inhabits the **large intestine** of humans, where it can cause ulceration of the intestinal lining.
 
• Clinical symptoms of the disease include **abdominal pain**, **constipation**, **cramps**, and the passage of stools characterized by **excess mucous** and **blood clots**.
 
• The transmission of the disease is facilitated by **houseflies** (Musca domestica), which serve as **mechanical carriers** by transferring the parasite from the feces of infected individuals to food and water supplies.

• **Cholera**:
 
 
• An acute diarrheal infection caused by the bacterium **Vibrio cholerae**.
 
• It is characterized by severe watery diarrhea, often described as **rice-water stools**, leading to rapid **dehydration**.

questions.question: The energy of light (photon) is a form of ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Electromagnetic Energy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Light** is fundamentally composed of **photons**, which are discrete packets or **quanta** of energy that lack rest mass but carry **momentum**.
 
• The energy of these **photons** is a manifestation of **electromagnetic radiation**, which occurs due to the synchronization of oscillating **electric** and **magnetic fields**.
 
• According to **quantum mechanics**, the energy (**E**) of a **photon** is determined by the **Planck-Einstein relation**: **E = hf**, where **h** is the **Planck constant** (approximately 6.626 × 10−³⁴ J·s) and **f** is the **frequency**.
 
• **Electromagnetic energy** covers the entire **electromagnetic spectrum**, including **visible light**, **infrared radiation**, and **ultraviolet rays**, all of which travel at the **speed of light** (approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum.
 
• Since light behaves as both a **wave** and a **particle** (wave-particle duality), its energy is transferred via **electromagnetic waves** that do not require a physical medium for conduction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nuclear Energy**

 
 
• Refers to the binding energy held within the **atomic nucleus**, typically harnessed via **nuclear fission** or **nuclear fusion** reactions.
 
 
 
• **Gravitational Potential Energy**
 
 
• A form of **stored energy** related to an object **mass** and its **altitude** or height within a **gravitational field**.
 
 
 
• **Mechanical Energy**
 
 
• Defined as the sum of **kinetic energy** and **potential energy** in a system, pertaining to **macroscopic** objects in motion or specific physical configurations.

__
 
• In **October 2025**, **Brazil** formally signed the **Multilateral Convention (MLI)** to implement measures related to the **Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)** project, specifically targeting the **Subject to Tax Rule (STTR)** and **Pillar Two** components.
 
• The **BEPS** initiative, led by the **OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework**, aims to prevent **multinational enterprises** from exploiting gaps and mismatches in tax rules to avoid paying tax in jurisdictions where economic activities are performed.
 
• By signing the convention, **Brazil** has committed to aligning its domestic tax legislation with international standards, facilitating its ongoing process for **OECD accession**.
 
• The **Multilateral Instrument (MLI)** allows countries to modify their existing **bilateral tax treaties** simultaneously to include anti-abuse provisions without the need for lengthy individual renegotiations.
 
• This move represents a significant shift for **Brazil**, which historically maintained a unique **transfer pricing** system, but has now transitioned toward the **OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines** to promote tax transparency and certainty.

• **Pillar Two**: Establishes a **Global Minimum Tax** rate of **15%** to ensure that large corporations pay a fair share of tax regardless of where they operate.
 
• **Subject to Tax Rule (STTR)**: A treaty-based rule that allows developing countries to "tax back" certain intra-group payments where these are subject to low nominal tax rates in the recipient country.

questions.question: Which feature separates the Malda Gap from the rest of the Ganga-Brahmaputra Plains?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajmahal Hills**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Malda Gap**, frequently referred to as the **Garo-Rajmahal Gap**, is a major geological depression that separates the main **Indian Peninsular Plateau** from its northeastern extension, the **Meghalaya Plateau**.
 
• This gap originated during the **Tertiary period** due to **down-faulting** of the crust, creating a tectonic rift that was subsequently filled with **alluvial sediments** carried by the **Ganga** and **Brahmaputra** river systems.
 
• The **Rajmahal Hills**, situated primarily in **Jharkhand**, represent the northeastern edge of the **Chota Nagpur Plateau** and serve as the physical western boundary of the Malda Gap.
 
• While the gap itself facilitates the merging of the **Ganga Plains** and the **Brahmaputra Plains**, the **Rajmahal Hills** act as the topographical feature that demarcates the transition from the stable peninsular block to the sedimentary depression. Hence, **Rajmahal Hills** is the correct feature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Meghalaya Plateau**:

 
 
• It consists of the **Garo**, **Khasi**, and **Jaintia Hills** and is geologically part of the **Deccan Plateau**.
 
• It serves as the eastern boundary of the **Malda Gap**, rather than the feature separating the gap from the plains.
 
 
 
• **Aravalli Range**:
 
 
• Stretching from **Gujarat** to **Delhi**, these are among the oldest **fold mountains** in the world.
 
• They are located in the western part of India and act as a divide between the **Thar Desert** and the **Ganga Basin**.
 
 
 
• **Bundelkhand Plateau**:
 
 
• Located in central India across **Uttar Pradesh** and **Madhya Pradesh**, it is characterized by **Archaean gneiss** and granite rocks.
 
• It lies to the south of the **Yamuna River** and is far removed from the Malda Gap region.

questions.question: According to the WMO report cited in 2025, global warming in Jan–Aug 2025 was approximately how much above pre-industrial levels?

__
 
• The **World Meteorological Organization (WMO)** analysis of global temperature data for the period of **January to August 2025** revealed that the global average temperature was approximately **1.42degreeC** above the **1850−1900** pre-industrial baseline.
 
• This measurement is derived from a synthesis of six major international datasets, including **NASA GISS**, **NOAA NCEI**, and the **Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S)**, which utilize millions of observations from ships, buoys, and land-based weather stations.
 
• The figure of **1.42degreeC** highlights a continuing trend where global temperatures are dangerously close to the **1.5degreeC** threshold defined by the **Paris Agreement** as a critical limit for avoiding the most severe impacts of climate change.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Pre-industrial Baseline**:
 
 
• The period **1850−1900** is used as a reference because it is the earliest period for which high-quality, global-scale instrumental temperature records are available.
 
• Warming relative to this period is the primary metric used by the **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)** to assess progress toward global climate goals.

questions.question: Which feature of the Brahmo Samaj best reflects its reformist interpretation of Hindu religious practice?

options.text: Reviving Vedic polytheism and encouraging ritual offerings across India.
Promoting monotheistic worship and rejecting ritual sacrifices entirely.
Upholding hereditary priesthood and strengthening caste divisions everywhere.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Promoting monotheistic worship and rejecting ritual sacrifices entirely.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Brahmo Samaj**, established by **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** in **1828**, was founded on the principle of **Monotheism**, which emphasized the worship of one single, formless God (the **Brahman**). This was a direct challenge to the prevalent polytheistic practices and deity worship in 19th-century India.
 
• The movement sought to reform Hinduism by returning to the original philosophical roots found in the **Upanishads** and **Vedanta**, arguing that these ancient texts supported a rational, ethical, and monotheistic framework rather than the complex ritualism that had developed over centuries.
 
• A central tenet of the Samaj was the total rejection of **idol worship** and **ritual sacrifices**. The members believed that God should be reached through **meditation**, **prayer**, and the reading of scriptures, rather than through external physical offerings or the mediation of a **priestly class**.
 
• By advocating for the removal of **meaningless ceremonies**, the **Brahmo Samaj** aimed to create a simplified and purified form of religion that was accessible to all, regardless of caste or social status, thereby promoting **social equality** and **humanism**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**:

 
 
• Known as the **Father of Indian Renaissance**, he founded the **Atmiya Sabha** in **1815** before establishing the **Brahmo Samaj**.
 
• He played a pivotal role in the abolition of **Sati** in **1829** through the efforts of **Lord William Bentinck**.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of the Samaj**:
 
 
• After Roy, the leadership passed to **Debendranath Tagore**, who introduced the **Brahmo Covenant**.
 
• In **1866**, the movement split into the **Brahmo Samaj of India** led by **Keshab Chandra Sen** and the **Adi Brahmo Samaj** led by Tagore.
 
 
 
• **Vedic Polytheism vs. Reformism**:
 
 
• While some later movements like the **Arya Samaj** emphasized **Back to the Vedas**, the **Brahmo Samaj** was distinct in its heavy reliance on the **rationalist** and **universalist** interpretation of the **Upanishads**.

questions.question: Which Amendment made written Cabinet advice mandatory for Emergency in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**44th Amendment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **44th Constitutional Amendment Act** was enacted in **1978** by the **Janata Party government** primarily to undo several changes made by the **42ⁿd Amendment** and to provide safeguards against future misuse of emergency provisions.
 
• Before this amendment, the **President** could declare a **National Emergency** on the oral advice of the **Prime Minister**, as witnessed during the **1975 Emergency** when **Indira Gandhi** advised the President without consulting her Cabinet.
 
• The act amended **Article 352** to stipulate that the **President** can only issue a **Proclamation of Emergency** after receiving a **written recommendation** from the **Union Cabinet** (the Prime Minister and other ministers of Cabinet rank).
 
• It replaced the vague term **'internal disturbance'** with **'armed rebellion'** as a ground for declaring an emergency, ensuring it cannot be invoked for simple political unrest or protests.
 
• The amendment also mandated that the proclamation must be approved by both **Houses of Parliament** within **one month** (reduced from two months) by a **special majority**.
 
• Therefore, the **44th Amendment** is the legislation that made **written Cabinet advice** mandatory for imposing an emergency in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **42ⁿd Amendment Act (1976):**

 
 
• Known as the **Mini-Constitution**, it was passed during the **Emergency** to centralize power.
 
• It added **Fundamental Duties** via **Article 51A** and inserted **Socialist**, **Secular**, and **Integrity** into the **Preamble**.
 
 
 
• **24th Amendment Act (1971):**
 
 
• Enacted to counter the **Golaknath case** judgment, it affirmed **Parliament's** power to amend any part of the **Constitution**, including **Fundamental Rights**.
 
• It made it mandatory for the **President** to give assent to **Constitution Amendment Bills**.
 
 
 
• **26th Amendment Act (1971):**
 
 
• This act formally abolished the **Privy Purses** and privileges of the former rulers of **Princely States** in India.
 
• It omitted **Articles 291** and **362** to ensure equality of status among all citizens.

questions.question: Nagarjuna Sagar Dam is constructed across which of the following rivers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Krishna**__.

• It is constructed across the **Krishna River**, which is the fourth-largest river in India in terms of water inflow and basin area.
 
• The dam is geographically located on the border between **Nalgonda district** in **Telangana** and **Palnadu district** (formerly part of Guntur) in **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• The foundation stone for this massive project was laid by the first Prime Minister of India, **Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru**, on **December 10, 1955**, and the dam was completed in **1967**.
 
• The project is named after **Acharya Nagarjuna**, a renowned **Buddhist philosopher** and scholar of the 2nd century AD, who established a center of learning at the site now submerged under the reservoir, known as **Nagarjunakonda**.
 
• The structure stands approximately **124 meters** high and features **26 radial floodgates**, facilitating irrigation for over **10 lakh acres** of agricultural land.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

• It is often called the **Dakshin Ganga** and hosts major dams like the **Jayakwadi** and **Sriram Sagar**.
 
 
 
• **Tungabhadra River**:
 
 
• A major right-bank tributary of the **Krishna River**, formed by the confluence of the **Tunga** and **Bhadra** rivers at **Koodli** in **Karnataka**.
 
• The **Tungabhadra Dam** near **Hospet** is a significant multipurpose project on this river.

• Originates from the **Bhimashankar** hills in the **Western Ghats** of **Maharashtra**.
 
• It is the most important **left-bank tributary** of the **Krishna River**, flowing through **Maharashtra**, **Karnataka**, and **Telangana**.

questions.question: From which month and year are the Corporate Average Fuel Efficiency (CAFE-3) norms scheduled to be implemented in India?
questions.solution:
__Concept:__

**Corporate Average Fuel Efficiency (CAFE)** norms are regulatory standards designed to reduce the **carbon footprint** of the automotive industry. These norms aim to lower the average **fuel consumption** (and thus **CO₂ emissions**) of a vehicle manufacturer's entire fleet. In India, these standards are notified by the **Ministry of Power** through the **Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)**.

The implementation of CAFE norms in India is divided into specific phases, each with progressively stricter targets for **fuel efficiency** and **emission levels**.

Given

Target Phase: **CAFE-3 (Phase 3)**

Calculation

To determine the implementation date for **CAFE-3**, we look at the timeline established for CAFE norms in India:

 
• **Phase 1 (CAFE-1):** This phase was implemented from **April 2017** to **March 2022**.
 
• **Phase 2 (CAFE-2):** This phase is currently in effect, having started in **April 2022**, and is scheduled to conclude in **March 2027**.
 
• **Phase 3 (CAFE-3):** Following the completion of Phase 2, the third phase of these efficiency norms is scheduled to begin on **April 1, 2027**.
 
• **Phase 4 (CAFE-4):** This subsequent phase is proposed to start after five years of Phase 3, beginning in **April 2032**.

The transition to **CAFE-3** in **April 2027** will require automobile manufacturers to further enhance **engine technology**, promote **hybrid vehicles**, and increase the share of **Electric Vehicles (EVs)** in their total sales to meet the stricter **CO₂** emission targets.

Final Answer: April 2027

questions.question: The Battle of Khanwa (1527) was fought between Babur and which of the following rulers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rana Sanga**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Battle of Khanwa** was a landmark military engagement fought on **March 16, 1527**, at **Khanwa**, located near **Bharatpur** in **Rajasthan**.
 
• The battle took place between the forces of the first **Mughal Emperor Babur** and a powerful **Rajput** confederacy led by **Rana Sanga** (Maharana Sangram Singh) of **Mewar**.
 
• **Rana Sanga** aimed to expel **Babur** from India and had gathered support from various **Rajput** chiefs and Afghan nobles, including **Mahmud Lodi**.
 
• **Babur** employed superior military technology, specifically **artillery** (cannons) and **gunpowder**, alongside the **Tulughma** tactical formation, which neutralized the numerical advantage of the **Rajput** cavalry.
 
• The Mughal victory at **Khanwa** was more decisive than the **First Battle of Panipat**, as it crushed the most potent internal threat to **Babur** and firmly established the **Mughal Dynasty** in **Northern India**.
 
• After the victory, **Babur** adopted the title of **Ghazi** to celebrate his triumph over the confederated forces.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ibrahim Lodi**:

 
 
• He was the last Sultan of the **Delhi Sultanate** belonging to the **Lodi Dynasty**.
 
• He was defeated and slain by **Babur** in the **First Battle of Panipat** in **1526**.
 
 
 
• **Sher Shah Suri**:
 
 
• The founder of the **Suri Empire** in North India, he was a brilliant administrator and general.
 
• He famously defeated **Babur**'s son, **Humayun**, in the **Battle of Chausa** (**1539**) and the **Battle of Kannauj** (**1540**).
 
 
 
• **Bairam Khan**:
 
 
• He was a prominent military commander and the **regent** for the third Mughal Emperor, **Akbar**, during his minority.
 
• He led the Mughal army to victory against **Hemu** in the **Second Battle of Panipat** in **1556**.

questions.question: Which pigment is responsible for the green color of plants?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chlorophyll**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chlorophyll** is the primary biological pigment found in nearly all photosynthetic organisms, including green plants, cyanobacteria, and algae. It is essential for the process of **photosynthesis**, which converts light energy into chemical energy.
 
• This pigment is concentrated within the **thylakoid membranes** of the **chloroplasts**, which are specialized organelles in plant cells. The presence of these organelles is the defining characteristic of the **Kingdom Plantae**.
 
• The green color of plants is a result of **chlorophyll** absorbing light mainly in the **blue** (wavelengths 430 nanometers) and **red** (wavelengths 660 nanometers) regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. It poorly absorbs **green light**, which is instead reflected or transmitted to our eyes.
 
• Chemically, **chlorophyll** features a **porphyrin ring** structure similar to the heme in hemoglobin, but with a **Magnesium** (Mg) atom at its center instead of iron. This magnesium core is critical for the excitation of electrons when struck by photons.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Anthocyanin**

 
 
• These are water-soluble vacuolar pigments that may appear **red**, **purple**, or **blue** depending on the **pH** levels.
 
• They are responsible for the vibrant colors of flowers like **hibiscus**, fruits like **blueberries**, and the changing colors of leaves in autumn.
 
 
 
• **Xanthophyll**
 
 
• Belonging to the **carotenoid** group, these pigments are responsible for **yellow** colors in nature.
 
• They act as **accessory pigments**, helping the plant absorb light frequencies that chlorophyll cannot and protecting the plant from **photo-oxidation**.
 
 
 
• **Carotene**
 
 
• These are orange-colored photosynthetic pigments that lack oxygen in their molecular structure.
 
• The most common form is **beta-carotene**, which is abundant in **carrots** and serves as a vital precursor for the synthesis of **Vitamin A** (Retinol) in the human body.

questions.question: In which year was the first "Sanskrit Commission" constituted?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1956**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Government of India** officially constituted the first **Sanskrit Commission** on **October 1, 1956**, to evaluate the state of **Sanskrit education** and research in the country.
 
• The commission was chaired by the renowned Indian philologist and linguist **Suniti Kumar Chatterji**, who was then the Chairman of the **West Bengal Legislative Council**.
 
• The primary mandate of the commission was to examine the existing facilities for **Sanskrit studies** in universities, secondary schools, and traditional **Pathashalas**, and to suggest measures for their improvement and coordination.
 
• The commission explored the significance of **Sanskrit** in the context of the **Official Language** policy and its role in the cultural unity of **India**.
 
• After conducting extensive inquiries and visiting various educational centers, the commission submitted its final, detailed report to the **Ministry of Education** in **1957**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Structure and Recommendations of the 1956 Commission**:

 
 
• The commission included notable members such as **Dr. S.K. Belvalkar**, **Dr. V. Raghavan**, and **Dr. R.N. Dandekar**.
 
• One of its major recommendations was the establishment of a **Central Sanskrit Board** to advise the government on matters relating to the promotion of the language.
 
• It proposed the integration of **Sanskrit** into the **Three-Language Formula** and suggested the creation of **Sanskrit Universities** to facilitate advanced research.
 
 
 
• **Satyavrat Shastri and the Second Commission**:
 
 
• A second **Sanskrit Commission** was later set up by the government in **2014**, headed by **Professor Satyavrat Shastri**.
 
• This commission was tasked with developing a fresh roadmap for **Sanskrit** education in the modern globalized context, building upon the foundations laid in **1956**.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional and Cultural Context**:
 
 
• **Sanskrit** is recognized as one of the **Classical Languages** of India and is listed in the **Eighth Schedule** of the **Constitution of India**.
 
• The **Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan**, now known as the **Central Sanskrit University**, was established following the spirit of the commission's recommendations to preserve and propagate **Vedic** and **Sanskritic** learning.

questions.question: Article 243ZI of the Indian Constitution empowers the State Legislature to make laws regarding co-operative societies. Which principle is NOT included in its scope?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Compulsory State supervision**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 243ZI** was inserted into the **Constitution of India** by the **97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011**. This amendment added **Part IXB**, which specifically deals with **The Co-operative Societies**.
 
• The article mandates that the **Legislature of a State** may, by law, make provisions for the **incorporation, regulation, and winding up** of co-operative societies based on specific democratic principles.
 
• The four core principles explicitly mentioned under **Article 243ZI** are **voluntary formation**, **democratic member-control**, **member-economic participation**, and **autonomous functioning**.
 
• The inclusion of these principles in the **Constitution** ensures that co-operative societies function as **self-governing** and **economically viable** institutions without undue external pressure.
 
• **Compulsory State supervision** is **not** included in the scope of **Article 243ZI** because the primary goal of the **97th Amendment** was to reduce excessive **government interference** and promote the **autonomy** of these societies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **97th Amendment Act, 2011** also introduced other significant changes:

 
 
• It added **Article 43B** to the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, which tasks the State with the **voluntary formation** and **professional management** of co-operative societies.
 
• It amended **Article 19(1)(c)** to include the **right to form co-operative societies** as a **Fundamental Right**.
 
• **Voluntary formation**: Ensures that individuals have the freedom to join or leave a society of their own **free will**.
 
• **Democratic member control**: Establishes that the board and management are **accountable** to the members through **regular elections**.
 
• **Autonomous functioning**: Protects the society from being a **State-controlled** entity, allowing it to manage its **internal affairs** independently.
